text.p: In the fight for Jerusalem, language is a weapon of choice and the media is the battlefield.

Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu has launched a fresh war of words with Palestinians over his decision to send in bulldozers to build houses for Jews on the southeastern edge of Jerusalem despite international condemnation.
On both sides, spin doctors staking a claim to the land have gone racing for their maps and political dictionaries.
The opposing camps have enlisted local journalists and opinion-makers into the ranks, leaving the foreign media to pick their way through the linguistic minefield in between.
The first point of dispute is over the very name of the site where Netanyahu has started to build.
He calls the hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem Har Homa, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat calls it Jabal Abu Ghneim.
The 6,500 houses that are to replace the pine trees on the hill are an "illegal settlement" for one side, a "Jewish neighbourhood" for the other.

Israeli cabinet ministers have rushed before television cameras to declare that the building will relieve a chronic housing shortage for Jerusalem's Jews and Arabs. They portray it as a social problem.
For the Palestinians the project is only political -- an attempt to lock the Arabs out of Jerusalem behind a ring of concrete that will split the city from the rest of the West Bank.
The project goes to the heart of the dispute over Jerusalem. The problem for outsiders is -- whose Jerusalem?
Is Jerusalem a united city, the capital of Israel, as Israelis maintain?
Or is it a divided city whose "Arab" eastern half is illegally occupied by Israel and claimed by Palestinians as the capital of their future state?
The Israeli media accept Israel's annexation of the eastern part of the city captured from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East war.
Israeli newspapers refer to "eastern Jerusalem" when talking of the Arab sectors but they do not dispute Israel's claim to be the sovereign power. For them the whole city is "Yerushalayim".
Palestinian media use the Arabic term for Jerusalem, "Al-Quds" (The Holy). Many Arabic-language newspapers abroad call it "occupied Jerusalem" and "Arab Jerusalem".
Most Western media try to skirt the linguistic undergrowth around the city rather than cut through it.

"I fudged this issue," admits veteran NBC correspondent Martin Fletcher. "If you say Jerusalem you can be accused of taking the Israeli position, if you say Arab East Jerusalem you can be accused of making a political statement on behalf of the Palestinians. I just try to avoid it."
CNN's Jerusalem bureau chief Walter Rodgers says he tries to avoid labels.
"We refer to East Jerusalem without sticking Arab or Jew in as a prefix, and then often after that we add 'a city which the Palestinians hoped would be their future capital'," he said.

The written press too, often goes in for sentence-long explanations rather than labels to avoid the pitfalls of brevity. But shorthand is useful and several news organisations stick tags such as "mainly" Arab before East Jerusalem.
This of course is debatable since Jews now slightly outnumber Arabs in the eastern sector, although even those figures are disputed.
"Normally, for the sake of brevity, we refer to 'annexed East Jerusalem' in reference to Israel's decision to annex that part of the city it captured," said Christopher Walker of The Times of London.
Some correspondents, who did not want to be identified, said their organisations had come under pressure from Jewish groups to drop terms such as "occupied" and "settlement" from Jerusalem coverage.
Few news organisations seem to have rigid style rules on Jerusalem, prefering to leave it up to their correspondents.
